<reason>Both sides argued well, but CON controlled the decisive comparison. PRO's strongest strategic move was the symmetry attack — "your liability regime needs the same treaty cooperation my ban does" — and CON answered it squarely and cleanly in [B4.1]-[B4.2]: prohibition only pays off if universal, whereas testing standards, deployment thresholds and strict liability up one's own chain of command bite unilaterally, on day one, with no signature but your own. That answer dissolved PRO's central turn and left CON's asymmetry claim standing at the end, which PRO's closing only re-asserted against rather than dismantled. CON also won the two examples PRO chose to stake ground on: the cluster-munitions convention was turned into evidence of the compliant-disarm asymmetry (major arsenals unsigned, both sides using them in Ukraine), and the BWC analogy was turned by noting it has no verification protocol and survives because bioweapons are strategically marginal, unlike autonomy. CON's pressure question forced PRO to define "meaningful human control," and while PRO gave a serviceable line (human designates target or target class), CON's follow-up squeeze — read broadly it permits most of what CON defends, read narrowly it bans exactly the machine-classification task where a machine that cannot panic or avenge may outperform a terrified teenager — went largely unanswered; PRO's "that's the ban working" bites the bullet without engaging the civilian-harm comparison. PRO did land real hits: the Phalanx/Iron Dome question exposed that CON's "no defence" scenario is prospective rather than demonstrated, and CON conceded this honestly, which limited but did not erase the damage. PRO also correctly pressed that emergent failure modes differ from minefields, though CON's reply that strict liability exists precisely for unforeseeable harm was the stronger legal point. Execution costs cut both ways: CON had two turns clipped for exceeding the cap, losing its final sentences twice; PRO repeatedly cited nonexistent reference IDs ([C1.5], [C2.7]) and mildly overstated CON's silence in the closing. Net: CON made the debate easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's answer to PRO's symmetry attack ([B4.1]-[B4.2]): unilateral regulation improves your own systems whatever adversaries do, while unilateral prohibition only handicaps you — which broke PRO's claim that asymmetry sinks both regimes equally. A close second was CON's turn of PRO's own cluster-munitions precedent against it by pointing to the non-signatory arsenals that matter.</best_rebuttal>
